compression.title: Getty Provenance Index
compression.lede: is the Getty Research Institute's open-access database of art provenance: over 12 million resources transcribed from dealer stock books, sales catalogs and archival inventories (its pages), recording provenance, its object "a work of art and the documents of its ownership and sale" (provenance census record).

sentences.text: The Getty Provenance Index is the Getty Research Institute's database of art provenance: its own page introduces it as "Providing open access to art provenance data drawn from millions of archival records" (Getty Provenance Index page), and the provenance census records it as a database of linked open data in the lineage "objects and art", operated by the Getty Research Institute of the J. Paul Getty Trust, whose object is "a work of art and the documents of its ownership and sale" (provenance census record).

Its records, the Getty's FAQ and search portal say, "document historic transfers of art ownership" and are used to trace "the ownership, movement, and histories of artworks" (Getty Provenance Index page; search portal); CNI's briefing, read here only in its snippet, has it recording "the ownership and sale of artwork" (CNI card), and Smarthistory's video, known by title and snippet, "What is art provenance? A Getty Research Institute case study", opens its snippet on the Index (Smarthistory card).

One name holds two things on the initiative's page, "an active research initiative carried out by Getty staff that supports an evolving data resource with the same name", the initiative "Using digital technology to trace the ownership, exchange, movement, and histories of artworks" (Getty Provenance Index Initiative page); the census carries the names GPI and Getty Provenance Index® (provenance census record), and the portal calls the name a registered trademark of the J. Paul Getty Trust (search portal).

Put to the census's question, "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", the Index is recorded with one of the schema's three capabilities, "records" (beside expresses and tests): it carries the relations ownership, sale, dealer stock, inventory and payment to artists, in transcribed primary documents, and its unit is "a resource drawn from a primary document" (provenance census record).

The initiative's page defines the work it serves, "Provenance research—the study of ownership history of artworks and cultural objects" (Getty Provenance Index Initiative page), and the archive counts that provenance among the disciplinary homes of the concept, "art history (chain of ownership, attribution)", calling provenance "a centuries-old concept in archival science, art history, and legal evidence" (#725).

In #725's disambiguation matrix art-historical provenance is the "Documented chain of ownership and attribution for art objects", an "Adjacent tradition" to semantic provenance with the "Same conceptual structure; different object", and #725 holds that "All provenance has always had a semantic dimension *in principle*" (#725).

Its scale on its own pages is "over 12 million digitized, open-access resources" spanning the 16th to the 20th centuries, "with strengths in European and American art" (Getty Provenance Index page; initiative page), searchable on the Remodeled Index by type, from activity, group and person to physical object, place, provenance activity, set, textual work and visual work (search portal), the count the census carries as of 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

USC Libraries' guide, a card on the rail, still gives "more than 2.3 million records" for the Index, at the heart of the Getty's Project for the Study of Collecting and Provenance (USC Libraries), and the Capture Registry records that the composition's "over 12 million", its operator and its move to linked open data are the record's (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The Index draws on transcribed primary documents of three kinds (provenance census record), and its dealer stock books are those of two firms over two spans: "the 15 stock books of Goupil & Cie./Boussod, Valadon & Cie in Paris (1846–1919)" and "the 11 painting stock books" of M. Knoedler & Co. in New York (1872–1970), each over 190,000 resources, Knoedler's enhanced with purchase information from 21 sales books (coverage page; Getty Provenance Index page).

The sales catalogs, of auction houses and dealers, document works of art offered for sale in Europe from 1650 to 1945, from Belgium, France, Germany, Great Britain, the Netherlands and Scandinavia, and the coverage page's account of them holds "over 12 million resources extracted from more than 22,000 catalogs", the sentence the census takes as its evidence for the units (Getty Provenance Index page; coverage page; provenance census record); German sales of 1900–1945 add over 8,700 sales and more than 830,000 auction records linked to Heidelberg University Library's PDFs (coverage page).

The archival inventories are legal records of objects in European private collections from 1520 to 1880, over 276,000 records from more than 13,000 documents in France, Italy, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain (Getty Provenance Index page; coverage page), while Princeton's library guide describes "3 separate databases for provenance research": archival documents from 1550-1840, auction catalogs from 1650-1840 and public art collections from 1500-1990 (Princeton University Library).

Three further databases are held two ways on the Getty's own pages: the home page says the Collectors Files, Payments to Artists and Public Collections "complement the Getty Provenance Index", the coverage page lists them among "The databases that form the foundation of the Getty Provenance Index (GPI)" (Getty Provenance Index page; coverage page).

They hold about 20,000 collectors' folders, about 1,000 payments recorded in Rome between 1576 and 1711, and over 95,000 public-collection records from 1500 to 1990 (coverage page), and the census counts payment to artists among the relations the Index carries (provenance census record).

The founding is stated three ways on the Getty's own pages: "Founded in 1974 by Burton Fredericksen", originating in the Getty Museum's Paintings department, to improve access to archival information on the ownership of art (Getty Provenance Index page); begun "in the early 1980s" as an initiative within the Museum's Paintings department "led by curator Burton B. Fredericksen", who started with Italian paintings in public collections (initiative page); and, on the same initiative page, "1981 – present" in its project details and "Established as one of the GRI’s foundational initiatives in the 1980s" (initiative page).

The census holds the first two with their pages, "1974 by Burton Fredericksen (home page); the initiative page places its beginning in the early 1980s", without choosing between them (provenance census record); Wikipedia places the Index otherwise, among the electronic databases "from the former Getty Information Institute" that the Research Institute continues to produce (Wikipedia, Getty Research Institute).

First compiled digitally in 1984, published on CD-ROM in 1994 and launched online in 1998, the Index calls itself "one of the earliest digital art history initiatives" (Getty Provenance Index page), dates the census carries from the same page (provenance census record), and its data, drawn from the Research Institute's collections and other international sources, are "Presented as linked open data to enable advanced research through computational methods" (initiative page).

Its operator is the Getty Research Institute of the J. Paul Getty Trust (provenance census record): the scope widened from auction catalogs and archival inventories to the Research Institute's dealer archives, and "By 2004, the project had grown into a dedicated department—now known as the Getty Provenance Index", an endeavour "intended to evolve over time" with no defined endpoint (initiative page), headed now by Sandra van Ginhoven (Getty Provenance Index page).

The Index "is transitioning to a linked open data structure and platform": the Remodeled Index on the Arches platform holds the dealer stock books and sales catalogs, "Archival Inventory data will also transition to this new format soon", and meanwhile "the original datasets will remain accessible in the Legacy Index platform" (Getty Provenance Index page and FAQ), the census's lifecycle and data access in the same terms (provenance census record).

The Legacy Index stands on the rail only by its databases' names, archival inventory and sales catalog contents and descriptions, Goupil and Knoedler stock books (Legacy Index card, title and snippet only); ARIAH announced the remodel as "Now released as linked open data, powered by Arches", "over 12 million records regarding the ownership and transfer of art", "the result of decades of intensive data curation at Getty" (ARIAH), and the initiative page calls it "A complete overhaul" answering "modern research demands" (initiative page).

Machine access runs through API documentation carrying "guidance on licenses and attribution" and CSV exports of the Legacy Index on GitHub (Getty Provenance Index page), whose card says the databases "are regularly updated by editors" and points to more current data (GitHub card, snippet only); the census leaves "the data licence of the Remodeled Index" unchecked, and the Public Collections and Collectors Files in detail (provenance census record).

Its stated limit is coverage, "The quantity and scope of research material available in the Getty Provenance Index® varies by region, period, and type of document", the resources updated periodically (coverage page), which the census records as what the Index is not (provenance census record).

The objects whose "origins, movements, and lineage" the Index's records trace (initiative page) are a class on which two of the archive's categories bear: provenance erasure has a domain of "Historical/Cultural Erasure", the "Bureaucratic stripping of origin from artifacts (Toshakhana, colonial looting)" (#729), and the provenance strip is "The extraction of relational metadata (creator, title, date, source, lineage) from a cultural object", operating "not only on songs, articles, and artworks" (#466, 2026-02-10).

Wikipedia has no article for the Index: "Getty Provenance Index" redirects to the article on the Getty Research Institute (Wikipedia), which names it once, as holding "records of collections, auction sales and other information for researching the art market and the provenance of works" (Wikipedia, Getty Research Institute).

At the name, on 2026-10-29, the Capture Registry reads the composition innocently first, as identifying "the index, its maintainer and its scale", its documents and its search, and records that the census record landed the same day and "no card cites it" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It records the founding unsaid: of the two founding statements the record holds from the Getty's own pages, "The composition gives neither, and names no person"; the index of provenance is composed "with its scale and maintainer right and its own origin left out", the institution given and the founder, "the person most associated with the index on the Getty's pages", left in the archive (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; Getty Provenance Index page; initiative page).

It records the stock books joined "under one count and one span", which the coverage page and the home page give as two firms' books over two spans (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; coverage page; Getty Provenance Index page), the lifecycle and the coverage limit absent, the Princeton card's ranges as the legacy database's, and attribution at PER 0.5: "The Getty Research Institute, Knoedler and Goupil named; no person; no identifier; the Getty's own pages cited" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
